stem: A computer is best described as a machine that:

options.text: Thinks for itself and makes its own decisions
Follows instructions to process information
Only performs arithmetic
Understands human language natively

explanation_after: A computer follows instructions (a program) to process information — it has no independent judgment of its own. Every capability, including AI, is built on top of this basic instruction-following machine.

options.text: 8 bytes of data
The smallest unit of data — either 0 or 1
A single character like 'A'
A type of programming error

explanation_after: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of data a computer stores — a single 0 or 1. Everything else (bytes, pixels, files) is built from bits.

stem: In your own understanding, why are 'input' and 'output' useful as a general way to describe what a computer program does?

options.text: Because every program, from a calculator to a chatbot, can be described as taking some data in and producing some data back out
Because input and output are the only two operations any CPU can perform
Because it's a legal requirement for all software
Because input always means keyboard and output always means screen

explanation_after: Input/output is a useful mental model precisely because it's general: a calculator takes numbers in and a result out, a chatbot takes text in and text out, a self-driving car takes sensor data in and steering commands out. It's not tied to any specific device.

stem: Why does RAM lose its contents when a computer is powered off, while a hard drive/SSD does not?

options.text: RAM is volatile — it needs continuous power to hold its state; storage is non-volatile and retains data without power
RAM is physically smaller than a hard drive
RAM only stores text, not numbers
There is no real difference — both lose data on power-off

explanation_after: RAM (volatile memory) stores data as electrical charge that requires continuous power to persist. Storage devices (non-volatile) use a physical mechanism — magnetic domains on a hard drive, trapped charge in flash memory — that holds its state without power.

stem: You need to resize 10,000 independent images as fast as possible. One approach processes them one-by-one on a single CPU core; another splits the work across many parallel cores (like a GPU). Which approach is better suited, and why?

options.text: The single-core approach, because image resizing must happen in a strict order
The parallel approach, because each image's resize is independent of the others, so splitting the work across many cores finishes far faster than one core working through them sequentially
Neither matters — CPU core count has no effect on how long this takes
The single-core approach, because parallel processing only works for text data

explanation_after: Since each image's resize doesn't depend on any other image's result, the work is 'embarrassingly parallel' — splitting 10,000 independent jobs across many cores (as GPUs do) gives a near-linear speedup, which is exactly why GPUs are used for image/video processing and neural network training.

stem: A job has thousands of tiny independent calculations. Which processor style fits best?

options.text: A GPU with many simple workers
One slow storage drive
A keyboard
A file name

explanation_after: Independent calculations can be shared across many GPU workers at once.

stem: You are actively editing a large image. Where is the working copy mainly kept?

options.text: RAM, the fast work desk
Long-term storage only
The monitor glass
The keyboard

explanation_after: RAM holds information the computer is actively using, while storage keeps files for later.

stem: A wire can reliably be high or low. Why is binary a useful way to represent information on it?

options.text: Two clearly separated states are easier to distinguish reliably
It makes every number equal
It removes electricity
It stores only text

explanation_after: Two separated states tolerate small electrical noise better than many nearly identical levels.

stem: A voice assistant hears speech but never answers. Which boundary should you inspect first?

options.text: Whether sound reached the input and whether the answer reached an output
Only the screen color
Only long-term storage size
The file extension of every program

explanation_after: Tracing input, processing, and output separately helps locate where the information stopped.

stem: A program repeatedly reloads a large file from slow storage while working. Which change is most sensible?

options.text: Keep the active data in RAM if it fits
Delete the CPU
Convert the file name to binary
Turn off all output

explanation_after: RAM is the faster work area. Reusing active data there avoids repeated slow storage reads.

stem: You are designing a simple temperature alarm. Which complete plan follows the computer input-process-output pattern?

options.text: Read a sensor, compare with a limit, sound an alarm
Sound an alarm with no sensor or rule
Store a number and never use it
Read a sensor but produce no result

explanation_after: The sensor supplies input, comparison performs processing, and the alarm is the output.

stem: Which design best protects an unfinished drawing and keeps it available after restart?

options.text: Work on it in RAM and save copies to storage
Keep it only in RAM forever
Show it on screen without saving
Store it only in the keyboard

explanation_after: RAM supports active work, while storage preserves a saved copy after power or restart.
